resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1987 form describes the first (1797) tower as 30-ft brick; the 2011 form, drawing on a 1994 NPS historic structure report, says it was a 45-ft wooden octagon replaced by a brick tower under a 1831 contract. The 1857 present tower is the third. Wikidata/Rowlett's 1857 'tower 3' fits this.
1797 (1987 form, Rowlett) versus probably 15 January 1798 (2011 form); an old Truro man told Thoreau 1798.

notes_for_editor: Story rests mainly on the 2011 NRHP registration form (clean OCR) and the 1987 thematic nomination (letter-spaced OCR, quoted as OCR'd). The two disagree on the first tower (30-ft brick, lit 12 June 1797, vs 45-ft wooden octagon, probably lit 15 Jan 1798), the lens change (1945 vs 1946) and the demolition of the assistants' house (1961 in the 2011 summary, 1962 in its history); all are stated in the story. Thoreau does not name the keepers he met, so no keeper is named for his stay. The record's focal_height_m 51.8 and range_nm 14 are not supported by what was read; the 1987 form gives the tower as rising 120 ft above sea level (36.6 m) and the 1998 beacon as visible 20 miles. Roster: all principal keepers and numbered assistants from the USLHS list are included; the 'USCG' group (Coast Guard crew 1946-1971 and later, including Bernard Webber 1946-47) is not entered, as individuals may be living and the archive gives no roles. Kinship among the Small keepers (Isaac, James, Thomas K., Ernest H.) is not asserted. Portland newspaper: the Madison Daily Leader page was read via newspapers.py; OCR of the Portland Daily Press was too garbled to quote. Keepers in the Dolby note matched by roster years and the 1932 obituary. Wrecks other than Portland: none tied to the light by a source read. The Barnstable Patriot (1870) and Holbrook's statement are second-hand via LighthouseFriends. The Light-House Board volume labelled 1891-1892 is cited as the fiscal-1891 report because the lightning date (28 Feb 1891) and neighbouring June 1891 entries fall in it; printed page unconfirmed, scan page given. Not read: the 1994 NPS Historic Structure Report; Isaac M. Small's 1891 booklet; Light-House Board reports 1852-1890 (not in the corpus). Verification 2026-10-22: the 2011 form says only a portion of the ORIGINAL 1857 lens survives in the museum (the story had implied the 1901 lens); the cliff distance varies by source (75 ft in 1987 form, 143 [unit missing] in 2011 form citing a 1988 Corps study, 128 ft in LighthouseFriends for 1989); the 1987 chronology names Frances Small, not Isaac, as the 1796 seller; the 2011 form dates the Crouse-Hinds beacon 1946 (Section 8) and 1947 (Section 7). Sources 1 and 2 are the same PDF (1987 nomination followed by 2011 form), hence the same URL.
